intro.title: Classes and objects
intro.bodyMarkdown:
So far your data has lived in lists and dicts, and the code that works on it in separate functions. A **class** bundles the two together into a new type of your own. You've been using objects all along: `"hi"` is an object of the class `str`, and `"hi".upper()` is something that kind of object can do. Now you'll make your own.

```
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

rex = Dog("Rex", 3)
print(rex.name, rex.age)   # Rex 3
```

`class Dog:` describes what a dog is. Calling `Dog("Rex", 3)` makes a new dog, called an **instance** or **object** of the class. Python creates the empty object, then calls the special method `__init__` (short for "initialise"), passing the new object as the first parameter, `self`, followed by your arguments. `self.name = name` stores the value as an **attribute** on that particular object, reached afterwards with a dot: `rex.name`.

Every object gets its own attributes, so changing one dog doesn't touch another:

```
rex = Dog("Rex", 3)
fido = Dog("Fido", 5)
rex.age = 4
print(rex.age, fido.age)        # 4 5
print(type(rex).__name__)       # Dog
print(isinstance(fido, Dog))    # True
```

Class names use CapWords (`Dog`, `BankAccount`), while attributes are lowercase like other variables. `__init__` parameters can have defaults, just like a function's: `def __init__(self, name, age=0)` lets you write `Dog("Pip")`. Leave out a required argument and you get `TypeError: Dog.__init__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'age'`; read an attribute that was never set and you get `AttributeError: 'Dog' object has no attribute 'colour'`.

Why not just use a dict like `{"name": "Rex", "age": 3}`? A class gives every object the same shape, gives the type a name you can check with `isinstance`, and, from the next lesson on, holds the functions that belong with the data. You've actually written a class already: `class InvalidAgeError(Exception): pass` in the errors section made a new kind of exception.

One thing a plain class can't do yet is print nicely: `print(rex)` shows something like `<__main__.Dog object at 0x7f3a...>`. A later lesson in this section fixes that.

intro.title: Methods
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A **method** is a function written inside a class. You call it on an object with a dot, like `"hi".upper()`, and it works with that object's attributes. This is what makes classes useful: the data and the operations that keep it correct live in one place.

```
class Account:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self.balance += amount

    def describe(self):
        return f"{self.owner} has {self.balance}"

acc = Account("Ana")
acc.deposit(50)
acc.deposit(25)
print(acc.describe())   # Ana has 75
```

Every method's first parameter is `self`. When you write `acc.deposit(50)`, Python calls `Account.deposit(acc, 50)`: the object before the dot becomes `self`, and your arguments fill the other parameters. Inside the method, `self.balance` is that object's balance, so each account changes only its own.

Some methods **change** the object, like `deposit`, and usually return nothing. Others **answer a question** about it, like `describe`, and return a value without changing anything. Keeping the two kinds apart makes a class easy to use. A method can also call the object's other methods through `self`:

```
class Account:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance

    def can_afford(self, amount):
        return amount <= self.balance

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        if not self.can_afford(amount):
            raise ValueError("Not enough money")
        self.balance -= amount

acc = Account("Ben", 100)
acc.withdraw(30)
print(acc.balance)        # 70
print(acc.can_afford(80)) # False
```

Two mistakes come up a lot. Forgetting the `self` parameter, `def deposit(amount):`, gives `TypeError: Account.deposit() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given`, because Python passes the object as well as your argument. Forgetting `self.` inside a method, `balance += amount`, refers to a local variable that doesn't exist and raises an error.

An object can hold a list or dict as an attribute. Create it in `__init__`, so every object gets a fresh one of its own:

```
class Basket:
    def __init__(self):
        self.items = []

    def add(self, name, price):
        self.items.append((name, price))

    def total(self):
        return sum(price for name, price in self.items)

mine = Basket()
mine.add("tea", 2.5)
mine.add("cake", 4.0)
yours = Basket()
print(mine.total(), yours.total())   # 6.5 0
```

intro.title: Printing and comparing objects
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Out of the box, your objects don't print or compare in a useful way: `print(p)` shows `<__main__.Point object at 0x...>`, and two points with the same `x` and `y` aren't equal. Python fixes both with **special methods**, whose names start and end with two underscores (so they're nicknamed "dunder" methods). You never call them yourself; Python calls them when your object is printed, compared, and so on. `__init__` is the one you already know.

`__str__` returns the text `print()` and `str()` use. `__repr__` returns the text Python uses everywhere else: in the console, inside a printed list, and in error messages. By convention `__repr__` looks like the code that would make the object, so it's clear what you're looking at.

```
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __str__(self):
        return f"({self.x}, {self.y})"

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Point({self.x}, {self.y})"

p = Point(1, 2)
print(p)                # (1, 2)
print([p, Point(3, 4)]) # [Point(1, 2), Point(3, 4)]
print(f"{p} and {p!r}") # (1, 2) and Point(1, 2)
```

If a class only has `__repr__`, `str()` and `print()` use that too, so `__repr__` is the one to write first. Both must **return** a string; a `__str__` that prints instead fails with `TypeError: __str__ returned non-string`.

For `==`, Python calls `__eq__`. Without it, two objects are only equal if they are the very same object, like `is`. With it, you decide what equal means. When the other value is a different type, return the special value `NotImplemented`, which tells Python "I don't know how to compare with that" (and `==` then gives `False`).

```
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __eq__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Point):
            return NotImplemented
        return self.x == other.x and self.y == other.y

a, b = Point(1, 2), Point(1, 2)
print(a == b, a is b)    # True False
print(a == (1, 2))       # False
```

Defining `__eq__` has a side effect: objects can no longer go in a set or be dict keys, because Python can't be sure equal objects would land in the same place. Adding `__hash__`, returning `hash(...)` of the same values `__eq__` compares, brings that back. Only do it if the values won't change after the object is made.

`__lt__` (less than) is called for `<`, and it's all `sorted()` and `min()` need to put your objects in order. Return whether `self` should come before `other`.

```
class Version:
    def __init__(self, major, minor):
        self.major = major
        self.minor = minor

    def __lt__(self, other):
        return (self.major, self.minor) < (other.major, other.minor)

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"{self.major}.{self.minor}"

print(sorted([Version(2, 0), Version(1, 10), Version(1, 2)]))   # [1.2, 1.10, 2.0]
```

intro.title: Class attributes and class methods
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Attributes set on `self` belong to one object. A variable written directly inside the class body belongs to the **class** itself, and every object of the class shares it. That suits values that are the same for all of them, like a list of allowed sizes, and counts that span all of them, like how many have been made.

```
class Pizza:
    SIZES = ("small", "medium", "large")   # the same for every pizza
    made = 0                               # counts all pizzas

    def __init__(self, size):
        if size not in Pizza.SIZES:
            raise ValueError(f"No {size} pizzas")
        self.size = size                   # this pizza's own size
        Pizza.made += 1

Pizza("small")
Pizza("large")
print(Pizza.made)          # 2
print(Pizza("medium").SIZES)  # ('small', 'medium', 'large')
```

When you read `self.SIZES`, Python looks on the object first and then on its class, which is why every pizza can see `SIZES`. Assigning is different: `self.made += 1` would create a new attribute on that one object, hiding the shared one, and the class count would never change. To update a class attribute, assign through the class name, `Pizza.made += 1`.

```
class Robot:
    count = 0

    def __init__(self):
        self.count += 1     # makes a new attribute on this robot only

Robot()
Robot()
print(Robot.count)          # 0: the shared count never changed
```

The same sharing causes a classic bug with lists: `members = []` in the class body is **one** list that every team appends to. A list that each object should own must be created in `__init__`, as `self.members = []`.

A **class method**, marked with `@classmethod`, receives the class instead of an object, by convention as `cls`. Its usual job is an extra way to create objects, often from a different kind of input. Calling `cls(...)` makes the new object, just as calling the class does:

```
class Temperature:
    def __init__(self, celsius):
        self.celsius = celsius

    @classmethod
    def from_fahrenheit(cls, f):
        return cls(round((f - 32) * 5 / 9, 1))

    @staticmethod
    def is_freezing(celsius):
        return celsius <= 0

t = Temperature.from_fahrenheit(212)
print(t.celsius)                      # 100.0
print(Temperature.is_freezing(-3))    # True
```

A **static method**, marked with `@staticmethod`, gets neither `self` nor `cls`. It's an ordinary function that lives in the class because it belongs with it, like a check on a value before an object is made. Both kinds are called on the class itself, `Temperature.from_fahrenheit(212)`, without needing an object first.

intro.title: Keeping objects valid
intro.bodyMarkdown:
An object should never get into a state that makes no sense: a bank account with a negative balance, a person aged -5, a product with no name. **Encapsulation** means the object looks after its own data. It checks values when it's created and whenever they change, and the rest of the program goes through its methods instead of changing attributes directly.

```
class Account:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        if not owner.strip():
            raise ValueError("Owner can't be empty")
        if balance < 0:
            raise ValueError("Balance can't be negative")
        self._owner = owner
        self._balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        if amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Deposit must be positive")
        self._balance += amount

    def balance(self):
        return self._balance

acc = Account("Ana", 10)
acc.deposit(5)
print(acc.balance())   # 15
```

Checking in `__init__` means an invalid object can never exist: if the values are wrong, the object is never made. Raise `ValueError` for a value of the right type that isn't allowed, and `TypeError` for the wrong type altogether. The error stops the mistake where it happens, instead of letting a bad value spread and cause a confusing failure later.

The underscore in `_balance` is a convention meaning "internal: don't use this from outside the class". Python doesn't enforce it, and `acc._balance = -100` would still work, but every Python programmer reads it as a warning sign. Outside code calls `acc.balance()` and `acc.deposit(5)`, which keep the rules.

A method that hands out a list or dict should hand out a **copy**. If `history()` returned `self._history` itself, a caller could append to it and change the account's records behind its back. `return list(self._history)` gives them their own list to do what they like with.

```
class Account:
    def __init__(self):
        self._history = []

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self._history.append(amount)

    def history(self):
        return list(self._history)   # a copy

acc = Account()
acc.deposit(20)
h = acc.history()
h.append(1_000_000)                  # changes the copy only
print(acc.history())                 # [20]
```

Two underscores at the start, like `self.__pin`, go one step further: Python renames the attribute to `_Account__pin` behind the scenes ("name mangling"), so `acc.__pin` raises `AttributeError`. It exists mainly to stop subclasses clashing with a parent's names, and isn't real security either. A single underscore is the everyday choice.

The payoff comes when the rules change. If accounts may now go 100 into overdraft, you change one check inside the class, and every part of the program that uses accounts follows the new rule.

intro.title: Data classes
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Many classes mostly hold data: a point, a contact, a transaction. For each one you write the same things: an `__init__` that copies every parameter onto `self`, a `__repr__`, an `__eq__`. The `dataclasses` module writes them for you. You list the fields with their types, and `@dataclass` does the rest:

```
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int

p = Point(1, 2)
print(p)                  # Point(x=1, y=2)
print(p == Point(1, 2))   # True
print(p.x + p.y)          # 3
```

Each line like `x: int` declares a field: its name and, after the colon, its type. The type is a note for readers and tools; Python doesn't check it, so `Point("a", "b")` still works. A field can have a default, `score: int = 0`, and fields with defaults must come after those without, just like function parameters.

A default that's a list or dict would be shared by every object, the bug from the class attributes lesson, so dataclasses refuse it. Use `field(default_factory=list)` instead, which makes a fresh list for each object:

```
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Basket:
    owner: str
    items: list = field(default_factory=list)

    def total(self):
        return sum(price for name, price in self.items)

b = Basket("Ana")
b.items.append(("tea", 2.5))
print(b.total(), Basket("Ben").items)   # 2.5 []
```

A dataclass is still an ordinary class, so it can have methods and properties like `total` above. To check values or work out extra fields after the generated `__init__` has run, add a `__post_init__` method; Python calls it straight afterwards.

Options in the brackets change what's generated. `@dataclass(frozen=True)` makes objects read-only (assigning a field raises `FrozenInstanceError`) and lets them go in sets and be dict keys. `@dataclass(order=True)` adds `<`, `>` and the rest, comparing the fields in the order they're written, so `sorted` just works.

```
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True, order=True)
class Version:
    major: int
    minor: int

versions = [Version(1, 10), Version(1, 2), Version(0, 9)]
print(sorted(versions)[0])           # Version(major=0, minor=9)
print(len({Version(1, 0), Version(1, 0)}))   # 1
```

`dataclasses.asdict(obj)` turns a data class into a dict, ready for `json.dumps`, and `Point(**d)` turns a dict back into an object. Reach for a data class when a class is mainly a record of values; when the behaviour is the point, like an account that guards its balance, a regular class is often clearer.

intro.title: Medium project: Parking garage
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Build the software for a small car park. Different vehicles pay different hourly rates, the garage has a limited number of spaces, and at the end of the day it reports who is still parked and what it has taken. Times are in hours, so `9.5` is half past nine.

Vehicles are a family of classes. `Vehicle` holds what they share: a number plate and a `fee(hours)` method that charges the class's `rate` for each hour or part of an hour (at least one). `Motorbike` and `Car` only change the rate, while `Van` also changes how the fee is worked out: it has a minimum charge, so it overrides `fee` and builds on the parent's with `super()`. The garage never needs to know which kind it has; it just calls `vehicle.fee(...)`.

`Garage` holds the parked vehicles (composition) and keeps the rules: no parking when it's full, no parking the same plate twice, no leaving before arriving. The last step feeds it a day's events as text:

```
park car AB-123 9.0      ->  Parked AB-123
park van VN-77 9.5       ->  Parked VN-77
leave AB-123 11.25       ->  AB-123 paid 7.50
leave XY-999 12.0        ->  XY-999 isn't parked here
```

intro.title: Hard project: Monster battle
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Build the rules for a turn-based battle between a party of heroes and a group of monsters. Everyone is a `Character` with health points (hp), an attack and a defense. Heroes can drink healing potions, and mages throw fireballs that ignore armour, so they are subclasses that add to and change what a character can do.

A hit does the attacker's attack minus the target's defense in damage, but always at least 1 (and never more than the target has left). A mage's hit costs 5 mana and does double its attack, ignoring defense; out of mana, a mage hits like anyone else. In each round, every living hero hits the first living monster, then every living monster hits the first living hero. A battle with a hero, a mage and two monsters starts like this:

```
Round 1
Ana hits Goblin for 6 (Goblin: 6 hp)
Mia casts a fireball at Goblin for 6 (Goblin: 0 hp)
Orc hits Ana for 4 (Ana: 26 hp)
Round 2
Ana hits Orc for 3 (Orc: 17 hp)
Mia casts a fireball at Orc for 8 (Orc: 9 hp)
...
```

Every rule lives in the class it belongs to: damage in `Character`, potions in `Hero`, fireballs in `Mage`, and turn order in `Battle`, which holds the two sides and doesn't care which kind of character it is moving. Nothing here is random, so every battle can be checked line by line.

questions.prompt: Attack 3 against defense 5. How much damage?
questions.explanation: Damage never goes below 1, so a weak attack still does something.

questions.prompt: A hero with 28 of 30 hp drinks a potion (+10). How many hp now?
questions.explanation: Healing stops at the maximum hp, so 28 + 10 is capped at 30.

questions.prompt: Why is nothing in the battle random?

choices.label: So every battle can be checked line by line

questions.explanation: With no randomness, the outcome is the same every time and can be checked.
